column2: The shadow rolled over and pressed the suckers on both knees against the smooth inner wall. Its domain unfolded, sending transparent ripples outward. The water stopped instantly, solidified and sealed by the domain. The figure clenched a fist and struck the pipe, shattering the water, the pipe wall, and the rock outside together, like an old boxing master performing some legendary stone-splitting technique. The water flowed again, and the enormous pressure squeezed the shadow out.
He swam gently onward, the sound echoing through a vast, dark space.

The Well of Oblivion, the lowest level of the Ice Cellar. Legend said the three goddesses of fate spun, stretched, and cut the threads of life here. This was the place where all things were erased. It was as silent as an ancient cavern, save for the omnipresent sound of water.

The shadow took out two flares, lit them, and tossed one into the air. It crossed the darkness like a blazing meteor, yet could not penetrate the heavy blackness overhead. This was an immense underground cavern, carved by running water over tens of millions of years. The flare fell into the water ahead and went out.

The figure held the remaining flare high, illuminating his surroundings. The floor was bronze. Deep grooves, entwined like snakes, had been etched into it, and greenish-blue water flowed through them. Together they formed a flourishing vine that branched, branched again, then endlessly divided and rejoined before emptying into the silent lake ahead. Viewed from above, the shadow stood at the vine's root. Countless symbols appeared and disappeared among its tangled branches, forming a perfect circular totem around the little lake.

Here, in a place where no sky could be seen overhead and metal served as the earth beneath, time seemed frozen, everything sealed away and cut off. No wonder there were no elaborate defenses: the metal vine beneath his feet was the strongest defense of all.

An extraordinarily powerful domain filled the entire space, generated by the metal pattern underfoot. The vine was an unparalleled Yanling array. It was a miracle of alchemy: symbols and elements alone had created a domain, flowing and circulating without end. No living being was needed to sustain it. This was a privilege of the gods, beyond the reach of any religious code.
“So humans can take the art of alchemy to such extremes too,” the shadow murmured.

Where the lines on the floor tangled most densely, small domains formed strange circles full of power, suppressing the restless forces within. Each held a different exhibit: unfamiliar machinery, stone caskets covered in incantations, even the dried upper half of a mummy, its arms locked by bone shackles to a section of iron pillar. Mummy and pillar were immersed in formalin in an ultracold quartz-glass container. A metal plaque said it had been unearthed in 1836 in Egypt's Valley of the Kings, part of a pharaoh's burial goods.
“A junk heap.” The shadow glanced over the collection, any item in it capable of shaking the world.

He cut his wrist, and thick blood dripped into the grooves. Heavier than the greenish-blue water, it sank to the bottom and spread with the current. A new color stained the vine: the dark red of blood. Gradually the blood beneath the water began to glow in shifting colors, and bubbles rose to the surface as if from a violent chemical reaction. Soon the water boiled, bubbles and droplets dancing together. The Yanling array had been activated. Blood-red light flashed on and off in a steady rhythm, like a heartbeat.
The shadow's deep chant filled the entire space. Beneath that ancient, magnificent Yanling, the bloody light grew stronger, until the metal vine glowed like red-hot iron.
The light abruptly went out. Dark-red steam rose from every groove at once as the greenish-blue water evaporated; the dry channels looked as though strong acid had eaten through them.
The alchemical domain had been destroyed. The sealed space was free again, and everything felt light and fresh. Then... it was as if a host of demons had begun to dance!

The exhibits came alive, each in its own way. A bronze mask opened and closed its lips soundlessly, as if singing an ancient priest's hymn. The mummy writhed on its iron pillar, seemingly trying to break its shackles. The fine gold sand in a dark-gold hourglass had long since fallen to the lower chamber, but now an unknown force drew it back up. A mottled music box began to play again. Tiny new projections appeared on the silver cylinder that recorded its sounds: this was an entirely new tune.
A place meant to erase everything, a place like a coffin, had suddenly grown as lively as a temple fair.
“Shut up!” the shadow snapped.

His reprimand swept through the cavern like a military order. Wherever it reached, the exhibits trembled and fell silent again. Living spirits dwelled within them, and scarcely awakened from sleep, they felt a pressure more terrifying than eternal slumber: the pressure emanating from the shadow.
“You, keep playing.” He pointed to the music box. “Give us something grand. This should be a great reunion.”
The music box made several odd noises, perhaps tuning itself. Then a magnificent march rang through the space, solemn as the booming of an ancient bell.

The shadow walked slowly forward into the pool, where the greenish-blue water and the blood fought their final battle. He waded through calmly; the boiling liquid could not harm him. He looked straight ahead like a pilgrim approaching a shrine.

A circular metal altar stood in the center of the pool. He climbed onto it and looked at what lay before him. “We meet again. I still remember our covenant sealed in blood, and the oath to fight beside you until our blood ran dry. Yet when I see you again, you have withered away.”

They were the bare bones of a boy, dark bronze in color, like a work of art cast in solid copper. Crystallized eyes sat in the skull's sockets like a pair of golden glass marbles. The skeleton resembled a human's, but closer inspection revealed enormous differences. Its body contained nearly a thousand slender bones, some fused together, others forming structures found in no textbook. Two fans of delicate bones spread from its back: his wings. His outstretched arms gripped the wing bones behind him, and his skull hung low, like Jesus nailed to the cross.
A dragonbone cross.
The shadow stroked the skeleton. “You can't have died just like that, can you? This is no death for a Dragon King... Let me undo your last bonds.”

With one stroke he opened every artery in his wrist, and thick, fishy blood poured into the pool. For an alchemical domain, the greenish-blue water was like the electrolyte in a battery. Its circulation supplied an endless flow of power, mimicking the cycles of the world: sun and moon crossing the heavens, rivers running over the earth. The last alchemical domain contracted around the altar. Blood and greenish-blue water fought desperately, and the pool boiled furiously, but the evaporating water consumed the blood too. The two forces were evenly matched.
“To bring you back, I have to pay a greater price,” the shadow murmured.

His ventricles and atria contracted with all their strength. He controlled his own heart, squeezing blood from his body in a way no human could. The blood slowly settled to the bottom of the pool. With a deafening blast, all the water shot skyward, forming a circular wall dozens of meters high! It was a green-blue downpour flying in reverse. The final alchemical domain collapsed; the immense force shrouding the altar suddenly dispersed. The last bond had been broken!
At that instant the mighty march reached its climax, as though Beethoven's spirit had possessed the box and the heaven of the “Ode to Joy” had descended.
“Get up, Constantine!” The shadow clapped and roared.
No one answered. The dragonbone cross remained still, showing no trace of life. Green-blue spray fell on the skeleton like a sudden drizzle.
The shadow gazed silently at the skeleton. At last he stepped forward and gently gathered it into his arms, as a mother holds an infant. “Constantine... so you really are dead.”
“Play us a lament.” The shadow pressed his cheek against the skull.

The grand march stopped dead. Music of the deepest sorrow and chill poured from the music box's curved brass tubes, like Tchaikovsky's Pathétique mingled with the religious gravity of a Bach Mass. A soprano aria rose, piercing and beautiful, singing in a language not of this world of time turning like autumn leaves, of meetings often brief and farewells often eternal, of grief beyond human endurance being the world's eternal law.
“Perhaps because they know no dreams, the displaced pursue illusions,” someone sang softly and desolately, as though playing a dust-covered xylophone.
The shadow turned. Another figure stood in the darkness nearby, with an exquisite, curvaceous figure and splendid long legs.
“Oh, I didn't mean to interrupt. Just trying to match the mood,” the newcomer said with a soft laugh. Clearly a girl, she had a clear, ringing voice with a hint of insolence.

The first shadow fell silent for a moment and understood his situation. He had not heard the other approach; with his bloodline advantage, he could not possibly have failed to notice. There was only one explanation: she had been waiting there all along. She already knew what he was doing. “Mai Sakatoku?” He released the Dragon King's bones and rose slowly.

“Hi! Am I really that famous?” She snapped her fingers, and a light shone down from above. Mai Sakatoku stood lazily in its beam, arms folded, dressed in a black bodysuit, two straight swords strapped along her thighs, her long hair tied in a high ponytail.
“I came to pay my respects to a friend. What are you doing here?” The shadow kept his head down. Mai Sakatoku was clearly a dangerous opponent, but he showed no sign of caution.

“Stealing, of course. Who wouldn't want a look inside the Well of Oblivion, where the dragonbone cross is kept? Its defenses were too tight, though; blundering in would get you caught. But somehow part of the barrier suddenly failed. Like the lock falling off a granary door: naturally, we mice all rushed in. Paying respects to a friend? You're just another mouse here to steal. I'm the first, you're the second...” Mai Sakatoku suddenly turned toward the darkness to one side. “And he's the third.”
As if in answer, a third person's breathing sounded in the dark.
“How interesting. One more person and we'd have a full mahjong table,” the shadow said.
“Oh, we have enough for mahjong,” a voice said behind him, a hand raised high.
“Nice to meet you all.” Mai clapped, and a spotlight fell on each of the other three shadows.

The moment had come for everyone to show their true faces. Murderous intent hung taut as a drawn string, ready to snap at a touch! All three figures tensed in attacking stances... except the last, who wore a KFC paper bag over his head. Though his upright bearing and powerful muscles made a striking impression, the bag was a little out of place.
“Could you be a little more professional?” Mai burst out laughing.
“Do I have to dress formally?” Mr. KFC pointed to the third person. “Like him?”

The third person wore a light-gray suit, a white Florentine shirt, and, remarkably, a silver-gray neckerchief. He looked as though he had just come from a reception. He swept his bangs aside, revealing striking two-colored eyes, gold and sea blue.
“Let me introduce him,” Mr. KFC said. “This is Mr. Parsi Gattuso, secretary to the investigation team.”
“Just call me Parsi,” he said mildly.
“I must say, you're awfully polite for a thief. If I'd known someone like you would be here, I'd have worn an evening gown,” Mai said with a smile.

“No. Of the people here, I alone am not a thief. Everything in this college belongs to the Board of Trustees, including the dragonbone cross. The Board has authorized me to oversee its property. Naturally, I have no need to sneak around while inspecting what is mine to supervise,” Parsi said mildly.
“How wonderfully righteous,” Mai said with a grin. “But judging by the mud on your shoes, you don't seem to have come through the visitors' entrance. Did you cross the so-called 'garden'?”
Parsi looked down at his exquisite Italian leather shoes, now thoroughly coated in organic sludge. “Yes. It was difficult going.”
“And it looks as if you swam in? Didn't the sharks get in your way?” Mai turned to the shadow beside the dragon's bones.
The figure was a woman, dressed in a pure-black combat suit whose elastic fabric outlined her graceful curves. She stood straight as a crane.
“They're all asleep,” the woman said.
“Now that everyone's here, shall we begin?” Mai asked. “Does everyone at the table know how to play mahjong?”
“Sure, sure. Take from the player on your left, watch the one on your right, and keep a sharp eye on the one opposite,” Mr. KFC said confidently.

As he spoke, he slowly backed away, muscles swelling all over his body, blue veins slithering along his arms like little snakes. Generally, the greater a Yanling's power, the smaller its domain. With a high-risk Yanling like Sovereign Flame, the domain was only five meters across unless it exploded. Before the mahjong match had even begun, Mr. KFC had retreated to a comparatively safe position. He was clearly a crafty fellow.
An unsettling disturbance in the air came from Parsi. No one had heard him chant, but his domain had already been activated.

This would be no easy game of mahjong. All their banter could not conceal the murderous intent. Anyone who dared break in here was desperate enough to risk death; they could not take apart the Dragon King's bones and divide them up, and there was no possibility of cooperation.
Mai remained languid, arms folded, not even touching the hilts of her swords.

“I'd say you're in the worst position. In mahjong, everyone should sit around the table; that's only fair. But you're sitting right in the middle,” Mai said to the shadow beside the bones. “You're closest to taking them, but we'll all attack you first. Would you like to step back a little too?”
“Right, she's trying to be the dealer!” Mr. KFC said.

But the shadow could not even be bothered to look at them. Head lowered, she gently stroked the dragon bones. “Mahjong is a fair game. Killing is not. It isn't a game, and it isn't fun. Before someone who holds authority and power, there is no such thing as an evenly matched fight. Weaklings like you can only die like insects!”
“My, my, are you going to finish all three of us in an instant?” Mai spoke lightly, but a shiver ran through her unnoticed.
“You sing beautifully. I liked it very much. 'Perhaps because they know no dreams, the displaced pursue illusions.'” The shadow spoke softly. “You poor creatures, chasing illusions.”
When she finished speaking, funeral bells pealed in unison!

Among the exhibits, a pipe organ two stories high suddenly began to play, a masterpiece with an alchemical mechanism at its heart. It played a Mass and a summons to the dead: the roar of ten million death gods gathered together! Everyone felt the impact from the shadow, not wind pressure or intense heat, but majesty! It was like a mountain slowly toppling toward you, about to crush you beneath it. A transparent domain visible to the naked eye spread outward from the shadow in every direction. The air curtain covered the Dragon King's bones gently and warmly; they did not so much as tremble. But the metal floor began to crack. Countless metal fragments rose slowly within the domain, accompanied by intense magnetization. The fragments clung to one another and revolved around the shadow like scythe-bearing death gods flying around a divine throne.
Five meters, ten, fifteen, twenty... The domain expanded rapidly. No one knew what the Yanling did, but death was surely the only possible end for anyone caught inside it.
But how could a Yanling so devastating also have such an enormous domain? It almost overturned the established rules of Yanling studies!
Twenty-five meters, thirty, thirty-five... It continued to expand. Flickering electric currents pierced the air within it, heating the suspended metal fragments red-hot.

Mr. KFC leaped backward over the circular pool beside the altar. It was not an escape, but the prelude to an attack. He began a low chant. His already imposing body swelled further, and his T-shirt slowly split. He raised an exhibit: a granite sarcophagus, an unidentified relic from the Maya era containing the remains of some unknown person of importance. An invaluable A-rank exhibit, it weighed three tons. A world champion weightlifter could lift only a little over two hundred kilograms; the visual effect was as astonishing as a worker ant raising fifty times its own weight.
Yanling: Bronze Throne.
The man's bones crackled softly, and a bronze sheen appeared on his skin. He hurled the sarcophagus high into the air!

It pierced the air curtain without slowing. A three-ton cannonball, it seemed certain to smash the slender shadow into a bloody pulp. But it suddenly stopped in front of her, as though an invisible hand held it aloft. The shadow struck its front with her fist, and a small crack appeared. Within seconds it spread to every corner of the sarcophagus. The coffin held its shape a few seconds longer, then the currents spinning within the air curtain blew it apart! Along with the important person's remains, it became a shower of drifting ash.

Everyone's expression changed. They all understood their mistake. This was not mahjong, but a slaughter. The shadow had initially been cautious only because the powerful alchemical domain was still active and restricting her. Now she had destroyed those shackles. Parsi drew an old flintlock pistol from inside his clothes, along with a brass box containing a bullet tipped with a carved dark-red crystal. The domain was not far away now, but he did not retreat; he loaded quickly. Retreat would have meant nothing. The shadow was playing cat and mouse with them, and she was perfectly capable of stopping the mice from escaping.
If the three mice wanted to live, they had no choice but to join forces and kill the cat!

A bullet tipped with the Philosopher's Stone: the supreme achievement of alchemy, pure spiritual element, transcending the four elements. The dragon monarchs and their descendants, who commanded the laws of the four elements, could issue no orders to an element beyond those laws. It was therefore invincible, able to pierce anything.
Parsi raised the pistol and fired. The dark-red bullet passed through the air curtain without resistance and struck the shadow.
The enormous impact drove her back a step, but she straightened again. Something like metal covered her body; the metal fragments had gathered over her. Dark-red crystal powder trickled down.
The bullet had shattered against her body!

“Didn't the person who gave you that bullet teach you how to use it?” the shadow said softly. “Once the spiritual element is refined into a crystal, it has a physical form. Its freedom from limitation applies only to Yanling. As a physical object, it will still shatter if it strikes something as tough as metal. You should have ambushed me, fired it into my body, and hit the core. That is how you could have killed me.”

The air curtain was only a few meters from Mai. Awed by its enormous majesty, she trembled faintly. Her Yanling was Dark Illumination; if she wanted to flee in a dark place like this, no one could detect her. But fleeing would do no good now. The Yanling unleashed by the shadow was like Death itself. Nothing could survive within its domain, and in the end that domain would cover the entire space!

Molten metal fragments gathered before her into a grotesque weapon bristling with branches, ten meters long and covered in radiating iron crystals. It was Death's great scythe! Mai had only her two ninja swords, each with a blade less than about two feet long.
The enormous scythe whistled through the air curtain. Mai was as fragile before it as a fledgling, about to have her heart pierced and be impaled on its metal barbs.
A hand reached out of the shadow behind Mai and grasped the scythe's edge!

It belonged to another shadow concealed behind her, a fifth person in the cavern. He held the red-hot metal as easily as if he were holding a cup of tea. The air curtain stopped advancing, its transparent edge of death thirty centimeters from his face.
He was an utterly ordinary-looking shadow, his face indistinct, his build unremarkable. He even seemed to be wearing pajamas.

“Authority and power? Do you believe in authority and power too?” The man in pajamas looked at the shadow. “Good. You understand the rules better than they do. But those who believe in these rules must also pay their price.”

“Mai, get up. Stand in front of me. You need not be afraid, and certainly need not panic,” he ordered coldly. “Here, one person has Bronze Throne as his shield and knows no fear; another has the Philosopher's Stone as his shield and knows no fear. You have neither, but you have me behind you.”

Mai rose and walked in front of him, her back to the man, standing between him and the boundary of death. If it advanced even a little farther, she would be crushed to powder like the sarcophagus. But she was no longer afraid, for the man had stepped out of the shadows.
“I understand. You are my shield,” Mai said.

“No. I am not your shield. You are my weapon. The sharpest weapon needs no shield; its edge is its shield. There is no need to defend. You need only cut down the enemy.” The man placed a hand on the back of Mai's head. “I grant you blood, to refine your soul in blood. What cannot be reached shall remain beyond reach, yet wherever you go, brilliance shall radiate! I grant you swords: slay all who defy you. Ame-no-Habakiri and Futsu-no-Mitama!”
A calm domain unfolded, like a tiny stone dropped into water. But that stone raised a towering wave!
Mai closed her eyes. When she opened them again, golden flames blazed in both pupils.
In an instant she had been transformed. A domain like the shadow's own, like Death itself, surged from her body and drove back the boundary of death pressing against her.
She drew both swords: Ame-no-Habakiri in her left hand, Futsu-no-Mitama in her right!

Mr. KFC and Parsi could no longer tell whether what they were seeing was real or an illusion. These were two of the three spirit swords from Japan's so-called Age of the Gods. Futsu-no-Mitama was the sword of the thunder god Takemikazuchi, while Ame-no-Habakiri was the divine blade with which the Japanese god Susanoo slew the ancient eight-headed serpent Yamata-no-Orochi. In other words, they should not exist as real weapons at all; they held a place like the Chinese Golden-Hooped Rod.

Yet Mai really had drawn two long swords flowing with crimson and molten gold. Ame-no-Habakiri, true to its other name, the Ten-Grasp Sword, was a long curved blade ten fists in length. Futsu-no-Mitama was an enormous straight sword two meters long, exactly as in the legends.
“Only three people in all of history could rewrite a bloodline. Who are you? Who are you? Who are you?” the shadow asked hoarsely.

She had watched the man ever since he stepped out of the darkness. She had remained silent because she could not speak. More keenly than the other three, she sensed how terrifying he was—or rather, that he should not exist at all! His presence here was a greater paradox than Futsu-no-Mitama and Ame-no-Habakiri! At last she could not help asking, and the repetition betrayed the trembling deep in her soul.
“You're as beautiful as ever,” the man said with a soft laugh. He vanished like a trace of ink washed away by water.

Death's scythe shuddered and gave a dying wail. It was breaking apart, metal splinters shooting at Mai like blades, yet they could not cut her skin. They only severed the red cord binding her hair. Her black hair spilled loose like a waterfall and streamed out against the domain of death. She swung Ame-no-Habakiri with an effortless motion. It was the simplest of cuts, without any technique, like slicing an onion with a kitchen knife, yet Death's scythe disintegrated, fragments shooting back the way they had come. It was unparalleled strength, like the shadow destroying the sarcophagus.
Mai swung again. Futsu-no-Mitama traced a perfect arc around her, and within that arc a domain arose of its own accord. Dazzling violet electricity streamed over it with a thunderous roar.
Carrying a long sword in each hand, Mai advanced slowly into the shadow's domain. Across the surface of the newborn violet domain, two different currents crossed, sparks flaring and dying.
“An alchemical domain!” Parsi hissed.

Like the domain in the Well of Oblivion, the one Futsu-no-Mitama had activated was alchemical. It required no living host, only an alchemical object, and could circulate without end. Once, this had been a miracle imagined by alchemists, not an actual technique. A domain was created by a Yanling, and only living things could use Yanling. However carefully alchemy refined the elements, whether turning silver to gold or refining sulfur from volcanic ash, the result was lifeless matter. An alchemical domain was different. To achieve it, an alchemist had to reorganize the four basic elements into something possessing the essence of life, something alive and capable of releasing a domain.
But this was an act of stealing divine authority, a technique for imitating life from dust.
A forbidden art!
Apparently, every dogma existed only to be challenged and rewritten.

The two drew closer. The shadow's combat suit split, and blue-gray scales covered her beautiful body. It swelled abruptly, the scales rising like a field of steel thorns! Bone spikes pierced her skin: her black bones were growing toward the surface and becoming sharp blades. Molten metal fragments adhered to them and cooled, forming metallic crystals over the bone blades. The same transformation was taking place in Mai.
“Draconic transformation,” Mr. KFC said, licking his lips.
Ame-no-Habakiri roared, exultant. Another twisted metal weapon formed in the shadow's hand. They charged head-on like colliding meteors.
Endless light and heat, thunder and fire burst in every direction. The ground shook. Fragments of concrete crashed down around them; their first impact destroyed the exit from the Well of Oblivion.

Parsi raced into the black passage, the thunder behind him pursuing him like the death knell of the world! He had begun retreating before the two collided. Only a madman would stay; to watch a battle between gods, one had to be at least a demigod. This was an emergency passage leading to the enormous botanical garden through which he had infiltrated. Suddenly a jet of flame lit up his eyes, and a violent current hurled him away. Two figures flashed through the fire, weapons clashing, demolishing the concrete passage!
Like savage dragons locked in combat—was this their true strength when their dragon blood erupted?
Parsi turned and ran back toward the Well of Oblivion. He had studied its map before infiltrating and considered every escape route, but now only one remained usable.

Mr. KFC was hopping up and down, frantically pressing the elevator's up button. He stared when he saw Parsi racing toward him. “Waiting for the elevator too?” This was an emergency elevator, activated by card only when the Well of Oblivion was on the brink of destruction. Parsi clutched the white card in his hand. Mr. KFC, on the other hand, held nothing. He was simply hammering the up button like an office worker afraid of being late. Yet the elevator really was descending.
Was it... facial recognition?
Parsi hesitated. “Hello.”
The tremors grew more violent. Flame and lightning shot through the air; wind and broken stone flew everywhere. The two men waited for the elevator side by side.
“Didn't expect this the first time we met. We really ought to have had a proper chat,” Mr. KFC said.
Parsi had no idea where the man's peculiar sense of humor came from. He could only nod. “At a moment like this, seeing a monster like you makes me feel I've found my own kind.”
“Exactly. Makes you want to exchange business cards.”
At last the elevator doors opened, and the two men who had been chatting a moment ago scrambled inside like wild dogs.

But a strange, chilling sound came from overhead: the reinforced concrete structure was splitting apart! An enormous precast concrete slab slowly dropped along a clean cut. Mr. KFC's muscles surged as he thrust it aside with both arms. The elevator doors were about to close. Parsi hesitated for an instant, then a black sheathed hunting knife slid from his sleeve, bracing the doors open. It gave Mr. KFC a few seconds to vault over the knife into the elevator like an agile gorilla.

Parsi withdrew the knife, and the doors closed at once. The sudden upward acceleration threw both men onto the floor. Another tremendous shock came from below, so violent that the elevator shook like a birdcage in an earthquake. Half its floor collapsed, exposing the steel framework. They looked down into the black shaft. Seconds later, flames filled the long, deep darkness. Trapped superheated air rose with the fire like an enraged fire dragon, the blast of heat cutting their faces like a knife.
Parsi grabbed Mr. KFC's shoulder. His domain expanded to cover them both.
Yanling: Dustless Realm.

Everything without permission was excluded from the domain, even heat. Flames shot upward through the elevator, burning everything combustible until only its blackened metal frame remained, still carrying them upward.
The torrent of fire finally burst through the concrete at the top and twisted into the shape of a dragon in the night sky before vanishing in a flash.

The elevator reached the top. Red light rolled everywhere across campus. The alarm bells shrieked like a great flock of flamingos crying out in their final moments. The earth shook, buried water pipes burst, high-pressure jets spouted like fountains, granite facing peeled from buildings, and the rooster statue atop Valhalla crashed down.
It was like the apocalypse written in prophecy, and before it every person was as small as dust.

After breaking through the ground, the flames erupted from the well in front of Valhalla, the college's foundation well. In the days before running water, students and teachers had drilled the first spring there. Swept by searchlights, two shadows sprang out of the well and fled in different directions like mice, without time to say goodbye.
As Cassell College tottered in the sudden upheaval, ten time zones away in Beijing, China, the earthquake bureau announced a low-intensity earthquake measuring 2.1.

Earthquakes of such low intensity were commonplace. Only people working on the upper floors of tall buildings in the central business district would feel a little dizzy, so the news was quickly overlooked.
Naturally, no one connected the earthquake with the incident ten time zones away.
The subway lights went out. A few startled cries sounded, and after several seconds the lights came back on. The drowsy Zhao Menghua opened his eyes.

The train rumbled onward. An announcement said it was only an unexpected power outage, everything was normal, and passengers should not panic. Zhao Menghua glanced at the route display above the door. Zhongguancun was the next stop, and his destination. He had drunk too much with a buddy the night before and slept in his dorm; now he was headed back to Peking University. If it weren't rush hour, he would never have squeezed into the subway with a crowd. Even without a driver to pick him up in Beijing, he could have taken a taxi.
He could stop and have his phone repaired on the way. He couldn't open his contact list; the memory card was probably damaged.
He suddenly froze, his gaze caught. The person in front of him wore a black backpack bearing a circular emblem: the half-decayed World Tree.

Zhao Menghua had first seen that emblem at the Cassell College interview, and a second time on Lu Mingfei's credit card. It was the college crest. The young man and woman standing side by side ahead of him must have come from that mysterious college. Zhao Menghua had searched online for information about Cassell, but found nothing. On the surface it appeared to be a private school for the wealthy, but whenever he tried to learn more, he found it wrapped in an invisible shell that kept him from looking closely.

The more he encountered that barrier, the more curious he became. More importantly, from Lu Mingfei to Nono to Chu Zihang, every person who had humiliated him had come from that college. They were his sworn enemies.
“Boqian, have you found any targets?” the boy asked in a lowered voice.
The girl shook her head. “A few people with the bloodline, but probably a very low proportion. I haven't sensed anyone releasing a domain. Is this really going to work?”
Zhao Menghua felt his ears stand up like a rabbit's, but he couldn't really understand what the two were talking about.
“Searching for a first-generation dragon on the subway? I have no idea who came up with this plan. Would a first-generation dragon ride the subway?” the girl complained under her breath.
“They can take all kinds of forms. Didn't one in human form appear on campus?” the boy said reassuringly. “The subway has the densest flow of people, and you're sensitive to bloodlines and domains.”
“But going through every subway station every day is so boring,” the girl sighed.
“We haven't been to every station,” the boy said, apparently trying to cheer her up. “There are at least two hidden ones you haven't visited.”
“Hidden?”

“Mm. Not every station is open to the public. Every time you get off at the terminus, doesn't the train keep going? There are stations farther on; they just don't appear on the map. Those are the hidden stations...” the boy said.
“Next stop, Zhongguancun,” the announcement said.
“Come on,” the girl said. “Let's transfer to Line 4 and keep searching.”

A thought struck Zhao Menghua, and he quietly followed them. They were acting suspiciously, and he wanted to know what they were doing. There were few people in the transfer passage. He jogged after the pair, shivering for no apparent reason.
The escalator descended slowly, the fluorescent tubes overhead flickering on and off.

Zhao Menghua glanced at the framed advertisements on the wall and was surprised to find they had all been removed, leaving empty spaces. Scraps of newspaper littered the floor, as if it hadn't been cleaned in years. The young man and woman walked and talked, their voices growing more distant. Zhao Menghua hurried forward, but could no longer see them, only faintly hear their conversation. He rarely rode the subway, so he looked up at a sign. He had a vague feeling something was wrong with it, but paid it no attention. The underground passage twisted and turned, and the farther he went, the more scraps of paper lay on the floor, as though a vehicle loaded with old newspapers had just passed through.

Ticket gates appeared ahead, though Zhao Menghua remembered that he had not left the station; a transfer shouldn't require another ticket. But there was only this way, and the pair must have gone through. He felt in his pocket: nothing but hundred-yuan bills, not even two coins for a ticket. The floor trembled faintly. A train must be coming in.

He looked around, saw no one, and steeled himself to crawl under the gate. No one challenged him, and secretly pleased, he ran to the platform just as the incoming train stopped. With a sharp clacking, rusted bearings turned and the doors opened.
Zhao Menghua looked up at the train, a chill coursed through his whole body, and he stopped dead.

Its lights were off. He couldn't see whether the darkness inside was crowded with people or completely empty, but suddenly he realized he was alone on the platform. At some point the voices of the young man and woman had vanished. All along he had thought there were a few other people scattered through the station; only now did he see it was utterly empty. It was as though everything before had been an illusion.
He had been the only person in this station from beginning to end!

The station itself was wrong too... Zhao Menghua slowly raised his head. Fluorescent tubes flickered. Massive columns supported a high vaulted ceiling above a terrazzo floor, and green-painted iron railings bordered the stairs. Everything looked both familiar and strange.
He suddenly looked down and saw “LINE 1” painted in red on the train's battered exterior.
Line 1? Zhao Menghua shuddered. How could a Line 1 train be here? Zhongguancun was on Line 4, where the trains were all new imports!

But the train wasn't the only thing wrong. The station looked like Line 1 too: Beijing's oldest subway, with its vast, empty Russian-style interior, cold wind blowing across the platform, fluorescent lights washing every face deathly pale.

Zhao Menghua held his head and slowly crouched down, his mind blank. He remembered the empty advertising frames, the scraps of newspaper, and the peeling paint on the signs. All the anomalies he'd ignored came back to him. As he went deeper into the station, traces of the modern world had been gradually erased. He had entered a Line 4 station in 2010 and emerged into a Line 1 station from the 1970s. The transition had been seamless, time drawn back little by little along the long corridor.
The subway train still waited, its open doors seemingly inviting its only passenger aboard.
Zhao Menghua backed away step by step. How could he get on that strange train? Who knew where it would take him? Heaven or hell? Heaven, my ass! He turned and bolted up the stairs.

The station was utterly empty. Zhao Menghua could not remember the way in, so he searched everywhere for signs. The normally crowded station now looked like an enormous maze. He understood why some claustrophobic people never rode the subway: however it was decorated with light and color, a station was an enclosed space isolating you underground. In this vast space were countless signs, every one pointing to the platform he had just left. Whenever he tried to go the other way, he saw only their backs, painted with huge red crosses and the words “NO ENTRY.”
There was no way out, as if anyone who came here would never leave...

Icy wind poured into the station from the stairway leading to the platform, like the greenish vapor that often bursts out when an ancient coffin is opened. He could think of nothing else and ran, thick dust dancing behind him. He dared not look back and did not see the changes there. White walls gradually peeled and yellowed; aluminum ceiling panels became old-fashioned plaster; LED lights hidden in recesses were replaced by pallid fluorescent tubes; the escalator turned into hard, cold marble steps after he passed. Greenish mist was infecting the entire station like a virus of time.
“NO ENTRY.”
“NO ENTRY.”
“NO ENTRY.”

The repeated red crosses and “NO ENTRY” signs flashed before Zhao Menghua's eyes. It was like taking a wrong turn while driving and hearing a GPS repeat in a stiff female voice: “You are on the wrong route. Please make a U-turn ahead... Make a U-turn... Make a U-turn...”

Like hell he would turn around now. Zhao Menghua kept his head down and ran. Perhaps it was his imagination, but the station seemed suddenly to have grown dozens of times larger. Its passages were as complicated as a spiderweb; each turn led to another long corridor. Legends crowded into his mind: in a tomb filled with accumulated resentment, for example, there were always paths that never ended. Grave robbers thought they were running for their lives, but to someone unaffected by the enchantment they were merely marching in place with exaggerated movements...
At last there was light ahead. A white sign painted in red read “PROCEED THIS WAY.”
Joy surged through Zhao Menghua. It was the only different sign he had seen along the way. He leaped up four or five steps and stood beneath the sign pointing toward the light...

A silent subway platform waited ahead, as though dust and time had sealed it away for decades. Scraps of newspaper covered the floor. On the walls, old ceramic-tile pictures promoted “Five Stresses, Four Beauties, Three Loves.” Aging fluorescent tubes flickered and popped. He felt ice crystals forming in his blood. He was back on the very platform he had struggled to escape.

He sank down beside the stairs and sat stunned for a long, long time. Then he gathered up scraps of newspaper and pieced them together strip by strip until he had an almost complete paper. The publication date was January 30, 1992.
Eighteen years ago!
